To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we identified loss-of-function mutations of GAS8, a gene encoding the DRC4 subunit of the N-DRC in three independent PDC-affected families.
GAS8 loss-of-function mutations cause PCD by affecting the N-DRC.
loss-of-function mutations of GAS8, which encodes the N-DRC protein DRC4, cause PCD.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of novel PCD genes and the elucidation of their functional relevance for human ciliogenesis and motility.
the genetic and molecular characterization of the N-DRC defect in PCD.
the identification of novel PCD-causing genes and the functional characterization of the encoded gene products.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
loss-of-function mutations of the GAS8 gene cause PCD by disrupting the N-DRC and thereby impairing the motility of respiratory cilia.
the N-DRC is a critical component for normal ciliary function.
the N-DRC defect causes PCD.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the identification of loss-of-function GAS8 mutations in PCD-affected patients provides the first evidence that defects of the N-DRC can cause PCD.
the N-DRC plays a critical role in the regulation of ciliary motility and that GAS8 mutations are a novel cause of PCD.
the loss of DRC4 function results in the loss of nexin link integrity, which is associated with impaired ciliary beat frequency.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the N-DRC, an essential component of the ciliary apparatus, can be disrupted by loss of the DRC4 protein, and that the N-DNC defect may account for a significant proportion of PCD patients with a normal TEM.

the identification of novel PCD genes and the elucidation of their underlying mechanisms is still an ongoing task and that PCD should be suspected even in the absence of a ciliary defect as detected by TEM.
